items.item: a string's immutability means every apparent in-place edit (concatenation, slicing, case change) actually allocates a brand-new string object and copies into it; the original is untouched

items.item: immutability is why a string can be used as a dictionary/hash-map key: a mutable key could change its hash after insertion and silently break the hash table's invariant

items.item: immutability also buys safe sharing between references, since neither can observe an edit the other made, because there are no edits — this is what makes interning equal strings safe

items.item: building a string by looping s = s + piece is Θ(k²) for k pieces because each + allocates a whole new buffer sized to the current total length and copies everything built so far into it — the same shape as a dynamic array that reallocates by exactly one element every time instead of doubling

items.item: a UTF-8 code point takes between one and four bytes; ASCII code points take exactly one byte and are byte-identical to ASCII, which is why UTF-8 stays backward-compatible with ASCII-only text and tools

items.item: indexing a UTF-8-encoded string by byte offset is O(1), but indexing by code-point ordinal is O(n) in general, because the byte offset of code point n depends on how many of code points zero through n minus one were multi-byte

at.step: Is indexing the nth character O(1)?

items.item: Go's s[i] indexes bytes directly in O(1), and the only code-point-aware traversal the language gives, for range, is defined to decode one UTF-8 rune per iteration — an O(n) walk by construction, not a missed optimization

items.item: Rust's str has no single-integer indexing operator at all, and byte-range slicing panics at runtime off a character boundary — the language chose to keep slicing O(1) by making it unsafe without already knowing where characters start

at.step: Two real languages, two real trade-offs

items.item: a structure that wants O(1) code-point indexing anyway pays for it elsewhere: a side table of code-point-boundary offsets, or a fixed-width internal representation that gives up UTF-8's space efficiency

at.step: Two real languages, two real trade-offs

items.item: CPython's own str type is not a counterexample to the quadratic-concatenation claim: it is internally fixed-width per string (PEP 393), so code-point indexing is already O(1) on str, and separately its interpreter has a refcount-based optimization that can mask the quadratic cost of naive concatenation — neither fact is part of the Python language, and examples.py measures the claim on Java instead for exactly this reason
